{{short description|Graph coloring problem on paths in a network}}
In [[graph theory]], '''path coloring''' is a type of [[graph coloring]] where colors (or ''[[wavelength]]s'') are assigned to a set of [[path (graph theory)|paths]] in a graph such that any two paths sharing an [[edge (graph theory)|edge]] receive different colors. The objective is typically to minimize the number of colors used. Path coloring is motivated by the problem of allocating optical bandwidth to communication requests in [[Fiber-optic communication|all-optical networks]] that utilize [[Wavelength-division multiplexing]] (WDM).<ref name="ckp06">{{citation
 | last1 = Caragiannis | first1 = Ioannis
 | last2 = Kaklamanis | first2 = Christos
 | last3 = Persiano | first3 = Giuseppe
 | chapter = Approximation Algorithms for Path Coloring in Trees
 | doi = 10.1007/11671541_3
 | url = https://cs.au.dk/~iannis/publ/B2-book06.pdf
 | title = Efficient Approximation and Online Algorithms
 | series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science
 | volume = 3484
 | pages = 74–96
 | publisher = Springer
 | location = Berlin, Heidelberg

== Definitions ==

Path coloring may refer to either the '''WA''' problem or the '''RWA''' problem.

In the '''wavelength assignment problem''' (or '''WA problem'''), the input consists of a graph <math>G</math> and a [[multiset|(multi)set]] of paths <math>P</math> already defined on <math>G</math>. The task is to assign colors to the paths in <math>P</math> such that any two paths sharing an edge in <math>G</math> receive different colors.<ref name="ej01">{{citation
 | last1 = Erlebach | first1 = Thomas
 | last2 = Jansen | first2 = Klaus
 | doi = 10.1016/S0304-3975(99)00152-8
 | issue = 1–2
 | journal = [[Theoretical Computer Science (journal)|Theoretical Computer Science]]
 | pages = 33–50
 | title = The complexity of path coloring and call scheduling
 | volume = 255
 | year = 2001| hdl = 2381/18057
 | hdl-access = free
 }}</ref>

This formulation is equivalent to [[Graph coloring|vertex coloring]] the [[conflict graph]] of <math>P</math>, which has one vertex for each path in <math>P</math> and an edge between two vertices whenever the corresponding paths share an edge in <math>G</math>.<ref name="ckp06"/>

In the '''routing and wavelength assignment problem''' (also '''wavelength routing problem''' or '''RWA problem'''), the input consists of a graph <math>G</math> and a set of ''requests'' <math>R</math>, where each request is a pair of nodes to be connected. For each request, the algorithm must both select a path connecting the two endpoints and assign a color to that path, such that paths sharing an edge receive different colors.<ref name="ej01"/>

The RWA problem thus decomposes into two subproblems: the '''routing problem''' of selecting a path for each request, and the WA problem of coloring the resulting paths.<ref name="ckp06"/>

In general graphs where multiple paths exist between node pairs, these subproblems interact, making RWA more complex than WA alone.

== Trees ==
In [[tree (graph theory)|tree]] networks, the path connecting any two nodes is unique. Therefore, the routing subproblem becomes trivial, and wavelength routing in trees reduces to the WA problem.<ref name="ckp06"/> For this reason, research on path coloring often focuses on tree topologies.

The '''load''' of an edge is defined as the number of paths passing through it, and the load of a set of paths <math>L</math> is the maximum load over all edges. The load provides a lower bound on the number of colors required.<ref name="ckp06"/>

== Undirected and bidirected variants ==
Path coloring can be studied in both undirected and bidirected (directed) settings:<ref name="ej01"/>

* In '''undirected path coloring''', the graph <math>G</math> is undirected, and paths are undirected. Two paths conflict if they share any edge.
* In '''directed path coloring''', the graph is ''bidirected'' (each undirected edge is replaced by two directed edges in opposite directions), and paths are directed. Two directed paths conflict only if they share a directed edge in the same direction.

The directed variant models networks where each physical fiber link has separate capacity for each transmission direction.

== Complexity ==
Path coloring is [[NP-hard]] for both undirected and bidirected [[Cycle graph|ring]] networks. For trees:<ref name="ckp06"/><ref name="ej01"/>

* Undirected path coloring in stars is equivalent to [[edge coloring]] of [[multigraph]]s and is therefore NP-hard.
* Directed path coloring is NP-hard even for binary bidirected trees.
* Path coloring can be solved optimally in polynomial time for trees of bounded degree or when the number of paths touching any node is <math>O((\log n)^{1-\varepsilon})</math> for some <math>\varepsilon > 0</math>.

== Approximation algorithms ==
For undirected trees, a greedy algorithm using [[edge coloring]] of multigraphs achieves an approximation ratio of 3/2, which is tight.<ref name="ckp06"/> An algorithm with absolute approximation ratio 4/3 and asymptotic approximation ratio 1.1 also exists.<ref name="ej01"/>

For bidirected trees, deterministic greedy algorithms achieve a <math>5L/3</math> upper bound on colors for paths of load <math>L</math>. Randomized algorithms improve this to <math>7L/5 + o(L)</math> colors for binary bidirected trees.<ref name="ckp06"/>

== Relationship to call scheduling ==
Path coloring is closely related to [[call scheduling]], which generalizes the problem by introducing bandwidth requirements and call durations. When all bandwidth requirements, edge capacities, and call durations equal 1, call scheduling reduces to the RWA problem, with colors corresponding to time slots.<ref name="ej01"/>
